passages.title: The Plant-Based Lunch Trial and the Plates Returned Uneaten
sentences: A school offered a plant-based lunch option to one grade for a single Friday.
Students could choose the new meal or the usual chicken meal when they arrived at the cafeteria.
Thirty-six students selected the plant-based meal, but twelve of those trays came back with much of the main dish uneaten.
Some organizers said the trial showed students did not like plant-based food.
A survey after lunch found that several students liked the taste but had taken the option only because the chicken line was long.
Others said the unfamiliar bean portion was larger than they expected.
The committee realized that unfinished food mixed together taste, portion size, and the reason students had selected the meal.
For a second trial, students ordered the option one day earlier and could choose a smaller or regular portion.
Fewer trays returned with large leftovers, although the committee still received mixed comments about the recipe.
The report compared both trials instead of treating one Friday as a final judgment.
It recommended testing more recipes before making a permanent menu change.
The committee learned that participation and leftovers need context before they can explain preference.
passages.fullTranslation: 学校はある学年に一度の金曜日、植物性の昼食を選べるようにしました。生徒は食堂に来たとき新しい食事か通常の鶏肉料理を選べました。三十六人が植物性料理を選びましたが、そのうち十二のトレーは主菜を多く残して戻りました。主催者の一部は、生徒が植物性食品を好まない証拠だと言いました。昼食後の調査では、味は好きでも鶏肉の列が長いから選んだ生徒が何人かいました。ほかには、慣れない豆料理の量が予想より多かったという声もありました。委員会は、食べ残しには味、量、選択理由が混ざっていると気づきました。二回目は前日に注文し、小盛りか普通盛りを選べるようにしました。大量の食べ残しは減りましたが、料理への感想はまださまざまでした。報告は一度の金曜を最終判断にせず、二回の試行を比べました。恒久的にメニューを変える前に、さらに別の料理を試すことを勧めました。委員会は、参加数や食べ残しから好みを説明するには背景情報が必要だと学びました。

slashRows.en: A school offered a plant-based lunch option to one grade for a single Friday.
slashRows.jp: 学校はある学年に一度の金曜日、植物性の昼食を選べるようにしました。

slashRows.en: Students could choose the new meal or the usual chicken meal when they arrived at the cafeteria.
slashRows.jp: 生徒は食堂に来たとき新しい食事か通常の鶏肉料理を選べました。

slashRows.en: Thirty-six students selected the plant-based meal, but twelve of those trays came back with much of the main dish uneaten.
slashRows.jp: 三十六人が植物性料理を選びましたが、そのうち十二のトレーは主菜を多く残して戻りました。

slashRows.en: Some organizers said the trial showed students did not like plant-based food.
slashRows.jp: 主催者の一部は、生徒が植物性食品を好まない証拠だと言いました。

slashRows.en: A survey after lunch found that several students liked the taste but had taken the option only because the chicken line was long.
slashRows.jp: 昼食後の調査では、味は好きでも鶏肉の列が長いから選んだ生徒が何人かいました。

slashRows.en: Others said the unfamiliar bean portion was larger than they expected.
slashRows.jp: ほかには、慣れない豆料理の量が予想より多かったという声もありました。

slashRows.en: The committee realized that unfinished food mixed together taste, portion size, and the reason students had selected the meal.
slashRows.jp: 委員会は、食べ残しには味、量、選択理由が混ざっていると気づきました。

slashRows.en: For a second trial, students ordered the option one day earlier and could choose a smaller or regular portion.
slashRows.jp: 二回目は前日に注文し、小盛りか普通盛りを選べるようにしました。

slashRows.en: Fewer trays returned with large leftovers, although the committee still received mixed comments about the recipe.
slashRows.jp: 大量の食べ残しは減りましたが、料理への感想はまださまざまでした。

slashRows.en: The report compared both trials instead of treating one Friday as a final judgment.
slashRows.jp: 報告は一度の金曜を最終判断にせず、二回の試行を比べました。

slashRows.en: It recommended testing more recipes before making a permanent menu change.
slashRows.jp: 恒久的にメニューを変える前に、さらに別の料理を試すことを勧めました。

slashRows.en: The committee learned that participation and leftovers need context before they can explain preference.
slashRows.jp: 委員会は、参加数や食べ残しから好みを説明するには背景情報が必要だと学びました。

passages.title: The Rooftop Solar Display That Showed Only Sunny Days
sentences: An environmental club made a screen showing how much electricity the school's rooftop solar panels produced.
The first display used four especially sunny days because their graphs were easy to read.
Visitors saw high midday peaks and several assumed the panels produced similar amounts every school day.
A science teacher asked why cloudy and rainy days were missing.
The club realized that choosing only clear examples made the system look more consistent than it really was.
They added one full week containing sunny, cloudy, and rainy weather and labeled each day.
The new graph showed strong production on sunny afternoons and much lower output under thick clouds.
A monthly total remained on the screen so visitors could still see the panels' overall contribution.
The explanation said solar output varied with conditions and did not promise a fixed daily amount.
Students also linked the display to weather records so future viewers could compare changes themselves.
The club kept the sunny-day examples but placed them inside the broader record rather than presenting them alone.
They learned that selecting only attractive data can hide normal variation even when every number shown is true.

passages.title: The Museum Replica Displayed without a Clear Label
sentences: A local museum displayed a bright red helmet beside photographs from a historic fire brigade.
The case label gave the year of the brigade but did not say whether the helmet itself came from that period.
Several visitors assumed they were looking at an original object from the photographs.
A volunteer later checked the collection record and found that the helmet had been made ten years ago for an educational program.
Its shape and color were based on an original helmet kept in storage, but it was a replica.
The museum did not remove it because visitors could safely handle the replica during guided sessions.
Instead, staff changed the label to say 'replica based on the 1952 helmet in our collection.'
A small photograph of the stored original was added beside the explanation.
Visitors could now compare the replica with evidence of the original without confusing the two objects.
The museum also reviewed other hands-on objects for labels that might create the same misunderstanding.
The exhibit became more transparent while keeping the useful teaching object available.
Staff learned that a replica can teach effectively only when visitors are told clearly what it is and what evidence it represents.

passages.title: The Historical Map with a Place Name That Later Changed
sentences: Students compared an old town map with a modern map while researching a former riverside factory.
The old map marked a place called Sakura Landing beside the river.
The modern map had no Sakura Landing, but it showed Sakura Park several hundred meters upstream.
Some students assumed the park had been built on the exact site of the old landing because the name was similar.
A city record explained that the landing closed in 1958 and that the park received the old district name when it opened in 1974.
The record included coordinates showing that the two sites were not the same.
Students returned to the old map and used a bridge that still existed as a fixed reference point.
That placed the former landing downstream from the modern park, near what is now a parking area.
The project labeled the two sites separately and explained why the shared name could be misleading.
Students also avoided saying the parking area itself had existed when the landing was active.
Their final map used dates and a surviving landmark to connect old and modern geography accurately.
They learned that a place name can move or be reused, so matching names alone does not prove matching locations.

sentences: A biology club surveyed butterflies in the school garden for ten mornings.
Every day, members began at the bright flower bed beside the south gate and walked the same route.
Their results showed many butterflies near the south gate and very few near the shaded north trees.
The club first planned to report that butterflies strongly preferred the south side of the garden.
Then a student noticed that the survey always reached the north side nearly twenty minutes later.
Butterfly activity could change as the morning warmed, so location and observation time had been linked together.
For another week, the club alternated starting at the north and south ends.
They still saw more butterflies near the sunny flowers, but the difference was smaller than in the first survey.
The report included both weeks and explained the route-order problem in the first method.
The club suggested repeating the study in another season before making a general claim about the whole year.
They learned that a sampling route can bias a result when place and time always change together.
Changing the starting point made their comparison more balanced without erasing the pattern they had actually observed.

passages.title: The Later School Start Trial and the Morning Bus Problem
sentences: A junior high school considered starting first period thirty minutes later for one month.
Students felt tired in early classes, so the health committee tested extra morning time.
The first proposal simply moved every morning activity and the first bell thirty minutes later.
A transport manager pointed out that the school shared buses with an elementary school whose schedule would not change.
If the same buses arrived thirty minutes later, they would still be carrying elementary students on part of the route.
The committee realized that a classroom schedule could not be changed without checking how students reached school.
It surveyed families and found that sixty-two percent used school buses at least three mornings each week.
Some families could drive later, but many said work schedules made that difficult.
The transport company could provide one extra bus, but not enough vehicles to copy the entire route system at a new time.
Instead of canceling the idea, the school designed a smaller trial for students on two routes that the extra bus could cover.
Participation was voluntary, and students on other routes kept the normal start so transport remained available.
Teachers compared attendance, first-period alertness surveys, and late arrivals for the trial group before and during the month.
Most participants reported feeling less sleepy, and late arrivals did not increase.
However, several families disliked having siblings at different schools leave home at more widely separated times.
Teachers warned that the volunteer group might differ from all students.
The report therefore did not claim that a later start was proven best for everyone.
It concluded that sleep-related benefits looked promising but transport capacity and family schedules were major limits.
For the next year, the school asked the bus company to study a route redesign before any larger experiment.
Families could comment on several start-time options instead of only one.
The school learned that start-time changes must fit transport, families, and trial limits.

passages.title: The Reusable Cup Deposit Trial at a Community Event
sentences: A community festival usually used thousands of disposable drink cups during one weekend.
Organizers proposed a reusable cup system with a two-hundred-yen deposit returned when visitors brought cups back.
They expected most visitors to return cups because they would want the money back.
Several food vendors worried that collecting, stacking, and counting used cups would slow already busy serving lines.
The first design placed return boxes at every drink stall.
During a small rehearsal, customers returning cups crossed the same space as people buying drinks, creating confusion.
Organizers realized that a good environmental idea could fail if the return process created too much work at the wrong place.
They moved returns to three separate stations near the main exits and assigned volunteers only to cup collection.
Vendors then needed only to hand out clean cups and collect the deposit with each drink sale.
At the first full festival day, 1,240 cups were issued and 1,083 were returned by closing time.
Missing cups still mattered because replacements used money and resources.
A short visitor survey found that some people had left through a small side gate where no return station was visible.
Others said they had not understood that cups could be returned at any of the three stations rather than only near the original vendor.
For the second day, organizers added return signs at every exit and printed the three-station rule on drink tickets.
The side gate also received a small collection point during the final hour, when many families left at once.
The return rate improved, while vendors reported no longer lines than under the old disposable system.
Volunteers did spend significant time washing and checking cups after the event, so the report included labor as well as waste reduction.
The next festival kept the deposit but budgeted a washing team and improved exit signs from the beginning.
Organizers learned that reuse needs convenient returns, clear information, and realistic staff work.

passages.title: The Community Repair Cafe and Who Could Take Part
sentences: A youth group proposed a monthly repair cafe where residents could bring broken household objects and learn simple fixes.
The first plan invited anyone to work directly with volunteer tools after signing a short form.
Experienced volunteers liked the open atmosphere, but the community center manager asked about children, electrical devices, and sharp tools.
The group realized that equal access did not mean every visitor should perform every repair without limits.
They listed common tasks and divided them by risk rather than by the age of the object owner.
Sewing a loose button and tightening a simple screw were placed in a guided low-risk area.
Repairs involving mains electricity, damaged batteries, gas, or high heat were excluded from public work tables.
Children could take part in low-risk work with a guardian and a volunteer present.
The group also noticed an access problem: all work tables in the first room were high and had fixed stools.
One volunteer who used a wheelchair suggested adding two lower tables with clear space underneath.
The organizers borrowed adjustable lamps and placed commonly used hand tools where they could be reached from seated positions.
For the first event, every object received a short safety check before a visitor entered a work area.
Volunteers wrote 'repair not attempted' on items that fell outside the safe rules instead of experimenting with them.
Forty-seven objects were brought in, and thirty-one received some safe repair or adjustment.
Seven owners learned to make a small repair themselves under guidance rather than simply handing the object to an expert.
Feedback supported learning, but visitors wanted clearer information before bringing heavy items.
The group added an online list of accepted and excluded repair types with photographs of examples.
It also allowed visitors to send a description in advance when they were unsure.

passages.title: The Farm Market Orders, Harvest Table, Cooler Capacity, Delivery Routes, and Time Rules
sentences: A school agriculture club planned to deliver vegetable boxes to three community markets on Saturday.
The club had to fill confirmed orders without carrying more chilled produce than its cooler could safely hold.
The harvest table listed forty boxes of tomatoes, twenty-eight boxes of lettuce, and thirty-two boxes of carrots ready by seven thirty.
Market A ordered twelve tomato, eight lettuce, and ten carrot boxes; Market B ordered fifteen, ten, and eight; Market C ordered ten, eight, and twelve.
The orders totaled thirty-seven tomato, twenty-six lettuce, and thirty carrot boxes, so the harvest could cover every confirmed order.
However, lettuce had to stay chilled, and the van cooler held only eighteen lettuce boxes at one time.
The route table showed twenty minutes from school to Market A, fifteen more to B, and twenty-five from B to C.
A time rule said all lettuce must reach a market within sixty minutes after leaving the school cooler.
At first, students planned to load all twenty-six lettuce boxes and visit A, B, then C in one trip.
That plan failed immediately because twenty-six exceeded the van cooler's capacity of eighteen.
They considered loading A and B lettuce together, which required exactly eighteen boxes.
The van could reach A in twenty minutes and B thirty-five minutes after leaving school, both inside the sixty-minute rule.
After delivering to B, the van would return to school to collect Market C's eight chilled boxes.
A different direct road from B back to school took twenty-five minutes, and school to C directly took thirty minutes.
That meant C's lettuce could leave school on the second trip and arrive thirty minutes later, safely inside the rule.
Tomatoes and carrots for C could wait in the covered loading area.
Students checked market opening times next: A opened at eight thirty, B at nine, and C at ten.
Leaving school at eight ten would reach A at eight thirty and B at eight forty-five, fifteen minutes before B opened.
The club changed departure to eight twenty-five, reaching A at eight forty-five and B at nine, while keeping both lettuce deliveries within thirty-five minutes.
After unloading at B, the van returned to school, loaded C's order, and left again after a short count check.
It reached C after ten, so the market was already open and no chilled box had spent more than thirty minutes outside the school cooler.
Every order matched the written sheet, and the two-trip plan stayed within harvest, cooler, route, and time limits.
The club learned to check quantity, storage, travel time, and opening rules together.
passages.fullTranslation: 学校の農業部は土曜日に三つの地域市場へ野菜箱を届ける計画を立てました。確定注文を満たしつつ、保冷庫の安全容量を超えて冷蔵野菜を運ばない必要がありました。収穫表では七時半までにトマト四十箱、レタス二十八箱、ニンジン三十二箱が準備できます。市場Aはトマト十二、レタス八、ニンジン十箱、市場Bは十五、十、八箱、市場Cは十、八、十二箱を注文しました。注文合計はトマト三十七、レタス二十六、ニンジン三十箱で、収穫量はすべてを満たせます。しかしレタスは冷蔵が必要で、車の保冷庫は一度に十八箱まででした。経路表では学校からAまで二十分、AからBへ十五分、BからCへ二十五分でした。時間規則ではレタスは学校の保冷庫を出て六十分以内に市場へ着く必要がありました。最初、生徒たちはレタス二十六箱を全部積み、A、B、Cを一度で回る予定でした。しかし二十六箱は保冷庫容量十八箱を超えるため、その案は成立しませんでした。AとBのレタスを合わせるとちょうど十八箱なので、それを一緒に積む案を考えました。学校出発からAは二十分、Bは三十五分で、どちらも六十分以内です。Bへ届けた後、車は学校へ戻りC用の冷蔵八箱を受け取ることにしました。Bから学校へ戻る別の直通路は二十五分、学校からCへ直接は三十分でした。つまりCのレタスは二回目に学校を出て三十分後に着き、規則内に収まります。C用のトマトとニンジンは屋根付き積込所で待機できました。次に開場時刻を確認すると、Aは八時半、Bは九時、Cは十時でした。八時十分に出るとAへ八時半、Bへ八時四十五分で、Bの開場十五分前です。出発を八時二十五分に変えるとAへ八時四十五分、Bへ九時で、レタスはどちらも三十五分以内です。Bで荷下ろし後、学校へ戻りCの注文を積み、短い数量確認後に再出発しました。Cへは十時過ぎに到着し市場は開場済みで、冷蔵箱は学校の保冷庫を出て三十分を超えませんでした。すべての注文が書面と一致し、二回配送は収穫量、保冷容量、経路、時間条件を満たしました。部は、数量、保管、移動時間、開場規則を一緒に確認すると学びました。

sentences: A junior high school planned a summer sports day with outdoor matches from nine in the morning until two thirty.
Two days before the event, the forecast showed higher temperatures than the school had expected.
A heat-index table listed 29 at nine, 32 at eleven, 35 at one, and 34 at two.
The school guideline called for extra breaks above 31 and moving hard outdoor activities to another time or place at 35 or higher.
The field map showed a large shaded gym entrance on the west side and a smaller tree area on the east.
Water Station A stood beside the gym, Station B was near the center field, and Station C was beside the east gate.
The original match table placed long-distance running at one and the soccer final at one forty.
At first, organizers planned to keep the schedule and simply add more reminders to drink water.
The planning team noticed that this would not follow the written guideline if the index reached 35 at one.
They moved long-distance running to nine twenty, when the forecast value was still below the extra-break level.
The opening program was shortened slightly, so runners still had time to prepare before the earlier race.
The soccer final was harder to move because both teams also had morning matches.
Organizers prepared an indoor skills final in the gym if the one-o'clock measured index reached 35 or above.
The gym had enough space for both teams and officials but not for every spectator.
A live screen was placed at the large shaded west entrance so additional spectators could watch from outside the playing area.
The shade map also showed that Station B in the center field had no nearby cover at midday.
A temporary canopy and benches were moved to Station B so students could drink while seated out of direct sun.
Each team received a scheduled water break after every match, and teachers kept a simple record of students using the cool rest room.
At twelve thirty, the measured index was 34, so low-intensity outdoor activities continued with the added breaks.
At one, the index reached 35 exactly, so the prepared change for hard outdoor activities was used.
The soccer final changed to the indoor skills format, while a relay planned for later was moved to a cooler practice day.
Families were told the changes followed the measured index and school guideline.
The final report recorded schedule changes, shade, water breaks, and three students who rested for the rest of the event.
The school did not call the day risk-free just because the revised plan worked.
Students learned to combine measured heat, activity level, shade, water, timing, and a change rule.
